title: Identify and respond to selected literary texts

lessons.title: What literary texts are
lessons.html:
Stories, poems and songs

A literary text is writing or speech that is made to entertain us, make us feel something or make us think. It is different from a form, a label or a delivery note, which only give facts. Literary texts include:

  • stories – short stories, novels, folktales and fables;
  • poems – including praise poems (izibongo or lithoko) that honour a person, a clan or even a fine bull;
  • songs – work songs, church songs, songs at weddings and funerals;
  • plays and drama – on stage, radio or TV;
  • proverbs and riddles – short sayings that carry wisdom.

Many of these come from oral tradition. Grandparents told folktales by the fire, and workers sang songs while harvesting or herding. They were spoken and remembered long before they were written down.

Why read and listen to literature?

  • It is enjoyable and relaxing.
  • It teaches lessons about life, like honesty, sharing and hard work.
  • It helps us understand other people's lives and feelings.
  • It keeps our culture and history alive.
  • It improves our reading, listening and language.

A proverb

A well-known saying in South Africa is "Umuntu ngumuntu ngabantu" – a person is a person through other people. It is short, but it carries a big idea: we need each other. On a farm, the team only succeeds when everyone helps.

Where to find literary texts

You can find them in library books, newspapers and magazines, on the radio, on TV, in church, at community events and on a phone. Some LMS lessons and workplace newsletters also include short stories and poems. Ask the librarian or a teacher to recommend something in your home language.

lessons.title: Understanding a story
lessons.html:
The parts of a story

Most stories have the same main parts:

PartQuestion it answers
CharactersWho is the story about?
SettingWhere and when does it happen?
PlotWhat happens? (beginning, middle, end)
ProblemWhat goes wrong or what must be solved?
Theme or lessonWhat is the main idea or message?

A short story to read

Every morning old Mama Zodwa walked to the dam with her two buckets. One bucket had a small crack, and by the time she reached home it was only half full. The cracked bucket felt ashamed. "Why do you not throw me away?" it asked. Mama Zodwa smiled. "Look at the side of the path where you are carried. I planted seeds there. Every day you water them, and now there are flowers all along the way." The cracked bucket looked, and saw yellow flowers shining in the sun.

Thinking about the story

  • Characters: Mama Zodwa and the cracked bucket.
  • Setting: a path between a farm home and a dam, in the morning.
  • Problem: the bucket thinks it is useless because it leaks.
  • Ending: it learns that it has been helping flowers grow.
  • Lesson: everyone has value, even if they are not perfect.

Notice that the bucket talks. In fables and folktales, animals and objects often talk and act like people. This helps the storyteller teach a lesson in a simple way.

Responding to a story

When you respond, you say what you think and feel. You can:

  • say whether you liked it and why;
  • say which character you liked best and why;
  • link it to your own life: "This reminds me of a worker on our farm who...";
  • retell it in your own words to someone else.

lessons.title: Poems, songs and sharing your response
lessons.html:
Reading a poem

A poem uses few words to paint a picture or share a feeling. Poems often use rhythm (a beat), repetition (repeating words) and images (word pictures). Read a poem slowly, and read it aloud – poems are meant to be heard.

A short poem

The rain has come, the rain has come,
it drums on the roof like a wedding drum.
The veld drinks deep, the dam is wide,
the calves run out with the cows beside.

Thinking about the poem

  • Topic: rain falling on a farm after a dry time.
  • Repetition: "the rain has come" is said twice to show joy.
  • Image: rain "drums on the roof like a wedding drum" – this compares the sound of rain to a happy celebration. A comparison using "like" or "as" is called a simile.
  • Feeling: happiness and relief.

Praise poems and songs

Praise poems are performed with a strong voice and often with movement. They praise the good deeds and character of a person. Work songs help a team keep the same rhythm while hoeing or loading, and make hard work feel lighter. When you listen to a song, ask: What is it about? How does it make me feel? Why do people sing it?

Sharing your response

You can respond to a text in many ways:

  • talk about it with a friend or in a group;
  • write a few sentences about what you liked;
  • draw a picture of a scene;
  • write your own short poem or story about your farm or village.

There is often no single right answer about how a poem makes you feel. Give a reason from the text for what you say: "I think it is happy because the calves run out to play."

Key points

  • Literary texts include stories, poems, songs, plays, proverbs and praise poems.
  • Stories have characters, setting, plot, a problem and a lesson.
  • Poems use rhythm, repetition and images such as similes.
  • Respond by saying what you think and feel, and give a reason from the text.
